## Umbrella

`AQU-440` remains the policy source and coordinator for replacing functional-looking syntax with functional semantics. The child issues separate evidence, decisions, and verification into independently completable outcomes.

Unsettled policy children are decision-first. They create narrower implementation follow-ups only when evidence selects a code or migration change. Existing canonical issues remain independent and are linked rather than duplicated or reparented.

### Child issues and preferred order

#### Establish the policy evidence

- [ ] [AQU-443](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-443>): classify every functional-programming-adjacent rule and override.
- [ ] [AQU-444](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-444>): define owned functional semantics and the ownership, mutation, and effect boundary profile.

#### Secure and measure semantic boundaries

- [ ] Complete the existing analyzer and rollout work in `AQU-414`, `AQU-438`, and `AQU-410` without moving that work into this issue.
- [ ] [AQU-447](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-447>): measure residual direct parameter-mutation coverage after `AQU-410`.
- [ ] [AQU-449](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-449>): decide whether ownership-aware mutable-identity escape enforcement is needed after `AQU-444`.

#### Set language-level policy

- [ ] [AQU-446](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-446>): choose and prove checked exhaustive union handling.
- [ ] [AQU-452](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-452>): justify or narrow function-form and callback-reference restrictions.
- [ ] [AQU-448](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-448>): justify or reclassify Promise-chain restrictions.
- [ ] [AQU-451](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-451>): decide error and absence modeling by boundary.

#### Narrow exceptions and ratchet verified guarantees

- [ ] [AQU-450](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-450>): narrow semantic override boundaries using the `AQU-443` inventory.
- [ ] [AQU-453](<https://linear.app/aquaticat/issue/AQU-453>): define shared semantic fingerprints and category-by-category ratcheting using `AQU-410`'s fingerprint identity.

The checklist records the preferred rollout order. Linear `blockedBy` relations are reserved for hard prerequisites, so independently valid policy work can proceed in parallel.

### Existing canonical work

* `AQU-410` owns promotion of the three extracted readonly effect rules and their acceptance gate.
* `AQU-414` owns foreign-provenance and related semantic-analyzer defects.
* `AQU-438` owns the remaining observer-retention and rollout-blocker record.
* `AQU-178` owns functional composition helpers and is only related ergonomics.

## Full source brief

The original source brief is retained unchanged for rationale, evidence, vocabulary, acceptance details, and non-goals.

## Summary

The repository's Oxlint policy is stricter than a conventional TypeScript lint configuration,
but much of that strictness controls functional-looking syntax rather than functional semantics.

The configuration successfully pushes code toward immutable bindings,
readonly parameter types,
functions instead of classes,
and declarative collection operations.
It does not yet consistently prevent mutation of caller-owned values,
mutable identities escaping through closures and containers,
or opaque effects crossing project-owned boundaries.
At the same time,
it bans several ordinary functional TypeScript idioms,
including arrow callbacks,
Promise chaining,
and common typed absence/error encodings.

The result is an unstable middle ground:
contributors pay a substantial migration and syntax cost,
but the rules do not yet provide the strongest benefits normally associated with functional programming:
local reasoning,
referential transparency at owned boundaries,
explicit effects,
and exhaustive handling of sum types.

This issue should decide what "functional programming" means for this repository,
separate semantic guarantees from stylistic preferences,
and create a staged policy that makes the semantic guarantees real before adding more syntax restrictions.

## Reader primer: what "functional" means in this issue

This issue does not propose turning TypeScript into Haskell,
banning every loop,
or eliminating every stateful subsystem.
A TypeScript application must perform I/O,
manage resources,
coordinate asynchronous work,
and integrate with host APIs.

For this issue,
functional-programming discipline has several separable dimensions.
They should not be collapsed into one label.

### Binding immutability

A binding cannot be reassigned after initialization.
Examples include `const` instead of `let` and no mutable module exports.
Binding immutability makes the name stable,
but it says nothing about the object named by that binding.

```ts
const state = { count: 0, };
state.count += 1;
```

`state` is an immutable binding over a mutable object.
A rule that requires `const` has not proved value immutability.

### Value and ownership immutability

Code cannot mutate an object owned by its caller,
or expose a mutable identity that a caller can mutate later.
Local mutation may still be acceptable when the mutable value is created,
consumed,
and sealed inside one ownership-known boundary.

```ts
function summarize(input: ReadonlyDeep<Input>): Summary {
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();
  // Local mutation can be acceptable if `counts` never escapes.
  return Object.freeze(buildSummary(counts, input,));
}
```

The important question is not whether `Map.set` appears.
It is whether mutable identity crosses the boundary.

### Effect transparency

A function's caller-observable effects are either proved from source,
described by a truthful contract,
or rejected as unresolved.
This includes direct mutation,
mutation through aliases,
retained callbacks,
getters,
proxies,
host capabilities,
and work scheduled after return.

### Functions and composition

Behavior is assembled from functions and explicit data rather than inheritance ladders and implicit object lifecycle.
Higher-order operations such as `map`,
`filter`,
`reduce`,
composition helpers,
and small named functions are ordinary tools.
Arrow syntax is not itself functional semantics,
and function declaration syntax is not itself imperative semantics.
The policy should judge the behavior before judging the spelling.

### Algebraic data and exhaustiveness

Finite states are represented as literal unions or discriminated unions,
and every state is handled.
Replacing an enum with a union improves the type model only when downstream handling is exhaustive.
An `if` chain with a fallback is not automatically exhaustive.

### Controlled escape hatches

Foreign host values,
generated declarations,
third-party contracts,
and state-machine internals need explicit boundaries.
An exception should describe why the semantic guarantee does not apply,
not provide a broad way around a difficult migration.

These dimensions are related,
but they are not interchangeable.
A codebase can have immutable bindings and still be highly stateful.
It can use `map` everywhere while allowing hidden effects.
It can avoid classes while exposing mutable closure state.
This issue is about closing those gaps deliberately.

## Repository-specific vocabulary

The readonly analyzer uses several terms that are not standard TypeScript terminology.
A new contributor needs these definitions before reading the rollout issues or the suggestions comment.

* **Deeply readonly** means every reachable property,
  element,
  collection view,
  and callable capability has been classified as readonly.
  TypeScript's built-in `Readonly<T>` is shallow and does not establish this by itself.
* **Project-owned value** means repository code controls the value's construction and behavioral contract.
  A type declaration being in the repository does not alone prove runtime ownership,
  and an external type can still describe a project-created value.
* `ForeignBorrowed<T>` is the marker from
  `@monochromatic-dev/ownership-marker-foreign-borrowed`
  for mutable values whose ownership is dictated by an external caller or runtime.
  It records provenance;
  it does not claim immutability and does not make unresolved behavior safe.
* `ForeignHostCapability<T>` marks an exact runtime-owned host capability
  after ordinary source and source-map inference cannot resolve its behavior.
  It is narrower than `ForeignBorrowed`
  and is valid only with a truthful effect contract for the behavior being accepted.
* `@mutates` is a TSDoc effect-contract tag naming the callable parameter whose reachable state may be changed.
  It documents known behavior;
  it cannot be used to invent an effect merely to silence the analyzer.
* **Effect summary** is the analyzer's cross-file description of mutation,
  invocation,
  retention,
  returned identity,
  and unresolved behavior for one callable.
* **Opaque effect** means the analyzer cannot inspect enough of a reached call
  to prove what it may do with caller-owned state.
  Opaque does not mean mutation was observed;
  it means the guarantee could not be proved.
* **Omission identity** records a callable the TypeScript bridge deliberately could not summarize,
  so a later cache load can distinguish a known bounded omission from corrupt or missing evidence.
* **Diagnostic fingerprint** is the complete set of `(rule, file, range, message)` records from one controlled sweep.
  Cold,
  warm,
  and worker-count comparisons use it to detect lost or unstable coverage.
* **Self-hosting override** is the scoped exemption
  that prevents the semantic analyzer from applying its own strict host-effect policy to the analyzer package.
  The package necessarily calls TypeScript semantic handles and Oxlint host APIs
  that it cannot inspect as ordinary project source.
* **Positive control** is a fixture known to violate one promised guarantee.
  A guard is not proved until removing or disabling it makes that fixture fail in the expected way.

The detailed ownership model is documented in
`package/oxlint-plugin/prefer-readonly-parameter-type/README.md` and
`doc/troubleshooting/oxlint-prefer-readonly-foreign-provenance.md`.

## How Oxlint policy reaches repository code

The root `oxlint.config.ts` spreads the shared configuration from
`@monochromatic-dev/config-oxlint`.
The shared source lives under `package/config/oxlint/src/`.

`package/config/oxlint/src/config-base.ts` enables the built-in
`correctness`,
`suspicious`,
`pedantic`,
and `style` categories,
turns warnings into a failing result through `denyWarnings`,
and loads the Unicorn,
TypeScript,
Oxc,
Import,
Promise,
and Node plugins.
It then spreads four explicit rule groups and eleven file-pattern overrides.

The shared configuration also loads five project-owned JavaScript plugins:

* `@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-no-restricted-syntax` for syntax and policy rules;
* `@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-prefer-readonly-parameter-type` for semantic readonly and effect analysis;
* `@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-stylistic` for layout and expression formatting;
* `@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-tsdoc` for declaration and effect-contract documentation;
* `@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-test-import` for shipped-artifact test boundaries.

Measured by importing the built shared configuration,
there are 225 explicit rule entries:
104 at `error`,
38 at `warn`,
82 explicitly off,
and one explicit allow setting.
Therefore 142 explicit entries are active before category expansion.
The current `oxlint --rules` output reports 406 enabled built-in rules.
The full workspace run reports 484 rules after the project JavaScript plugins participate.

Those counts are configuration-size measurements,
not functional-programming scores.
For example,
the active explicit entries include twenty TSDoc rules and fifteen project formatting rules.
A strict documentation or line-layout rule does not make runtime behavior more functional.

## What the current policy gets right

The complaint in this issue should not erase the substantial work already present.
Several parts of the policy are unusually serious about functional design.

### Binding lifetime is constrained

`package/config/oxlint/src/rule/restriction.ts` enables:

* `eslint/no-var`;
* `eslint/prefer-const`;
* `no-restricted-syntax/no-module-root-let`;
* `no-restricted-syntax/no-function-root-let`;
* category-provided `import/no-mutable-exports`.

The custom root-`let` rules are stronger than `prefer-const`.
They reject broad mutation scope even when a binding is genuinely reassigned.
Their diagnostics direct authors toward a `const`,
a tighter block,
a named helper,
an IIFE,
or a bounded local state machine.
That is a useful local-reasoning policy.

### Stateful object design is pushed toward composition

`no-restricted-syntax/no-class` recommends a factory returning a frozen object.
The migration guide in `doc/migration/no-class.md` explains how closure-private state,
readonly return types,
and `Object.freeze` replace broad `this`-based state and inheritance.
Error and Web Component classes retain explicit exceptions because host contracts require class semantics.

This policy can create deeper modules with smaller public mutation surfaces.
It is functional in architectural direction even though the private closure may still mutate local state.

### Data modeling favors types over runtime enums

`no-restricted-syntax/no-enum` and
`typescript/consistent-type-definitions: ['error', 'type']`
push code toward literal unions and type aliases.
`typescript/consistent-indexed-object-style: ['error', 'record']`
and the `no-switch` guidance prefer explicit data maps when a discriminant maps to a value.

These are good ingredients for typed functional design.
The remaining problem is exhaustiveness,
described later in this issue.

### Common in-place array operations are rejected

The enabled Unicorn rules reject mutating `.sort()` and `.reverse()` in favor of copying alternatives.
The shared config also allows and encourages array transformations such as `map`,
`filter`,
`reduce`,
`some`,
and `find`.
The project deliberately leaves Unicorn's bans on `reduce` and `forEach` disabled.

This is a sensible preference for immutable collection transforms where the operation naturally returns a new value.

### Readonly analysis is semantic rather than name-based

`@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-prefer-readonly-parameter-type` is not a shallow AST rule.
Its README describes TypeScript semantic types,
demand-driven cross-file effect summaries,
foreign ownership provenance,
source and source-map resolution,
collection observer relations,
and fail-closed unresolved boundaries.

The enabled `prefer-readonly-parameter-types` rule reports a mutable parameter
only when it can prove a deeply readonly replacement.
This avoids the common failure mode of suggesting `Readonly<T>`
when nested mutable state or callable capability remains reachable.

Issues #423,
#427,
and #453 show that the repository is treating semantic correctness,
cache determinism,
and diagnostic actionability as real engineering problems.
That is the strongest part of the current FP policy.

## Where the current policy is not good enough

### Binding immutability is being mistaken for value immutability

The strongest active rules stabilize names,
not values.
All of these remain possible in ordinary production code
unless another type or semantic rule happens to catch the exact path:

```ts
const options = { enabled: false, };
options.enabled = true;

const cache = new Map<string, Item>();
cache.set(key, item,);

function update(config: Config): void {
  config.value = computeValue();
}

function retain(input: Input): () => Input {
  return function currentInput(): Input {
    return input;
  };
}
```

The current built-in rule set does not enable `eslint/no-param-reassign`.
The project-owned `no-immediate-mutation` rule is a warning-tier rule over a deliberately narrow shape:
a declaration followed immediately by an assignment,
`Object.assign`,
or selected collection mutation that could have been folded into the initializer.
It does not claim to prevent general object mutation,
parameter mutation,
alias mutation,
or escape of mutable identity.

The custom `no-module-root-let` documentation explicitly recommends a mutable `Map`,
`WeakMap`,
`Set`,
or `WeakSet` as one replacement for a mutable module binding.
That replacement improves mutation locality because the binding no longer changes,
but it does not make the module pure.

The policy needs to say which guarantee it intends:
immutable names,
immutable values,
owned local mutation,
or no mutation.
Today those meanings are too easy to conflate.

### The rules capable of enforcing effects are still disabled

Only one of the semantic plugin's four rules is active:

* `prefer-readonly-parameter-types` is `error`;
* `no-readonly-parameter-mutations` is `off`;
* `no-opaque-parameter-effects` is `off`;
* `no-invalid-parameter-effect-contracts` is `off`.

The disabled rules are the ones that move the policy from "this type could be readonly" to questions such as:

* does this function mutate caller-reachable state despite a readonly declaration;
* does an unresolved call receive or retain caller-owned identity;
* is an `@mutates` contract missing,
  stale,
  or inconsistent;
* is an ownership marker redundant or invalid.

Issue #423 correctly retains ownership of promoting these three rules
from `off` directly to `error` after workspace remediation.
Issue #427 records the defects discovered while measuring that rollout.
Its latest implementation update says persistent omission identities,
producer attribution,
foreign observer provenance,
and cold/warm worker parity have landed.
Issue #453 records the remaining work:
observer-return retention is still conflated with opacity,
`flat` still lacks collection-specific guidance,
and the post-repair whole-workspace fingerprint and reviewed acceptance set do not yet exist.

This issue should not duplicate that implementation work.
It should state plainly that the current FP policy remains semantically incomplete
until #423's gate is satisfied or explicitly superseded.

### Some hard bans remove common FP syntax without proving better semantics

The following production rules are not semantic purity rules:

* `no-restricted-syntax/no-arrow-function`;
* `no-restricted-syntax/no-variable-function-expression`;
* `no-restricted-syntax/no-array-callback-reference`;
* `no-restricted-syntax/no-promise-catch`;
* `no-restricted-syntax/no-promise-finally`.

There are legitimate reasons behind parts of these rules.
Named functions improve stack traces.
An unknown-arity callback reference can trigger the classic `array.map(parseInt)` class of bug.
`using` can express resource cleanup more reliably than a forgotten `.finally()`.
`async`/`await` can make lifecycle and error paths easier to read.

Those reasons do not make the banned syntax non-functional.
Arrow callbacks are the standard lambda form in TypeScript.
A proved unary function reference is ordinary point-free composition.
Promise chaining is the language's built-in value-oriented asynchronous composition form.
Named function expressions can provide both lexical closure and stable stack identity.

The callback-reference rule already recognizes some proved unary functions and explicit `unary` or `binary` wrappers,
which is better than a blanket ban.
The policy should apply that same principle broadly:
retain restrictions that prevent a measured defect,
and remove restrictions whose only effect is forcing one spelling over another.

### Union modeling lacks a mandatory exhaustive consumer

The repository bans enums and encourages unions,
which is compatible with algebraic data modeling.
It also bans every `switch` statement.
Oxlint's TypeScript `switch-exhaustiveness-check` rule is enabled through the pedantic category,
but the project ban prevents owned code from using the construct that rule checks.

The suggested replacements are an `if`/`else` chain or a `Record` lookup.
Neither replacement is necessarily exhaustive:

```ts
type Status = 'idle' | 'running' | 'failed';

function label(status: Status): string {
  if (status === 'idle')
    return 'Idle';
  return 'Other';
}
```

This compiles when `running` and `failed` need distinct behavior.
The fallback hides missing cases.

A `Record<Status, string>` can be exhaustive when the key type is exactly `Status` and the object supplies every key.
The current rule does not require that exact shape,
and its own example uses `Record<string, number>` plus a fallback.

Before retaining a blanket `switch` ban as an FP rule,
the repository needs an equivalent checked mechanism:

* an exact discriminant-keyed `Record` with no fallback;
* an exhaustive helper whose unhandled value must be `never`;
* or an explicitly allowed exhaustive `switch`.

Without one,
the type policy creates sum types but weakens total handling of those sums.

### The error and absence model is deliberately not mainstream typed FP

`AGENTS.md` rule PP4 says to throw custom errors rather than return error codes,
null values,
or result types.
The no-nullish and optional-escape policy bans many ways to encode absence
and directs traveling absence toward a domain-specific `unique symbol` sentinel.
The `no-nullish-union` section of
`package/oxlint-plugin/no-restricted-syntax/README.md` additionally states that generic `Option`,
`Maybe`,
and `Result` wrappers are not accepted as absence modeling in this repository.

That policy may be right for this codebase.
Throwing can keep successful return types simple.
Domain-specific sentinels can preserve exact absence identity.
A generic `Option` wrapper can add ceremony where a local guard is clearer.

It is still a deliberate departure from typed functional error handling.
The policy should record it as such
rather than presenting every union-and-function restriction as one coherent FP direction.
Expected domain failures,
partial lookups,
and asynchronous cancellation may benefit from a typed value at a library boundary,
even if unexpected failures continue to throw.
This needs an explicit decision,
not an accidental outcome of several independent bans.

### Local imperative algorithms are accepted, but the boundary is implicit

`AGENTS.md` rule IMM prefers `map`,
`filter`,
and `reduce` over mutable state and imperative loops.
Rule ITR explicitly allows `for...of`,
counter loops,
and `while` cursors for linear input.
The root-`let` rule allows a helper that builds a result through mutation when it returns one local binding.
Source suppressions commonly justify parser cursors,
fixed-point convergence,
stream folds,
timers,
and state-machine latches.

These are reasonable exceptions.
A parser cursor or bounded convergence loop is often clearer and more efficient
than rebuilding immutable accumulator objects.
The problem is that the acceptance principle is distributed across prose,
rule heuristics,
and inline suppressions.

The policy should state one ownership rule:
local mutation is accepted when its scope is bounded,
its mutable identity does not escape,
and the public result is deeply readonly or primitive.
That would turn many apparent exceptions into one coherent semantic rule.

### Overrides weaken the policy at important proof boundaries

`package/config/oxlint/src/overrides.ts` deliberately relaxes rules for declarations,
tests,
configuration files,
and the semantic plugin's self-hosting package.
Some relaxation is necessary:
ambient declarations mirror external contracts,
and test frameworks dictate callback shapes.

The test override currently disables,
among other rules:

* `prefer-readonly-parameter-types`;
* `no-arrow-function`;
* `require-destructured-params`;
* several unsafe-type and style checks.

The declaration override disables the readonly preference,
enum ban,
rest-parameter ban,
and destructured-parameter requirement.
The semantic plugin disables its own readonly preference across its whole package
because self-application cannot prove the TypeScript and Oxlint host authorities it necessarily calls.

These boundaries are understandable,
but broad test exemptions matter because tests contain helper libraries,
fixtures,
property generators,
and orchestration code that can escape into production assumptions.
The issue should require each semantic FP rule to state whether tests are exempt because the guarantee is irrelevant,
because the framework owns the input,
or only because migration is unfinished.

## Current workspace evidence

### Full lint run

The following command was run on a clean checkout before this issue was opened:

```text
mise run lint:oxlint
```

Oxlint reported:

```text
Found 3911 warnings and 1387 errors.
Finished in 242.0s on 3018 files with 484 rules using 16 threads.
```

That is 5,298 reported diagnostics.
The aggregate is not an FP defect count.
Most reported diagnostics came from type safety,
artifact-test imports,
magic numbers,
and project formatting rules.
The run also included `.mjs` analysis files
because the shared ignore list excludes `**/*.js` and `**/*.cjs` but not `**/*.mjs`,
which contributed unrelated unsafe-`any` noise.

The rule-tagged output nevertheless gives a useful snapshot of FP-policy migration:

* 308 `no-arrow-function` findings;
* 80 `no-function-root-let` findings;
* 28 `prefer-readonly-parameter-types` findings;
* 16 `no-module-root-let` findings;
* 14 `no-array-sort` findings;
* 2 `no-array-reverse` findings;
* 1 `no-immediate-mutation` finding.

This matters because the repository is already paying a large migration cost
for syntax and binding rules before the stronger semantic mutation and effect rules are active.

### Committed suppression scan

A tracked-TypeScript scan,
excluding the shared config's ignored fixture,
deprecated,
generated,
and build-output paths,
found:

* 29 production disable directives for `no-function-root-let`;
* 4 production disable directives for `no-class`;
* 3 test disable directives for `no-class`;
* 1 declaration-file disable directive for `no-class`;
* no production disable directive for the readonly preference,
  arrow ban,
  enum ban,
  `for...in` ban,
  or `switch` ban.

The root-`let` suppressions primarily describe bounded parser cursors,
convergence loops,
stream accumulation,
and lifecycle latches.
That pattern supports an owned-local-mutation rule better than an unexplained collection of exceptions.

### Evidence limitations

This issue uses the configured rules,
current plugin documentation,
current GitHub issue state,
one full lint run,
and a static directive scan.
It does not claim that every reported finding is valid,
that every source file is reachable in production,
or that enabling the three extracted semantic rules today would be stable.
Issues #427 and #453 explicitly say the stable whole-workspace rollout fingerprint is still missing.

The purpose of the measurements is to establish direction and migration cost,
not to turn one noisy lint run into a purity score.

## Why this matters

### False confidence

A reader sees `const`,
readonly parameters,
no classes,
no enums,
and pervasive array methods and reasonably concludes that mutation and effects are tightly controlled.
That conclusion is stronger than what the active rules currently prove.
A functional-looking surface can hide mutable aliases,
retained callbacks,
container mutation,
and unresolved host behavior.

### Migration effort is aimed at the wrong layer

The workspace currently has hundreds of findings for arrow syntax and root binding scope,
while the three rules that reason about caller-observable mutation and unresolved effects remain off.
This ordering spends contributor effort on code shape before securing the semantic boundary.

### Rules can pull in opposite directions

Issue #422 recorded a concrete case
where replacing an immutable `Map` construction with a mutable record-building loop
satisfied the readonly analyzer while moving against the IMM preference for immutable functional transforms.
The current rule design has improved since that issue,
but the example demonstrates why each rule must be judged by the semantic outcome of its recommended repair.

### Onboarding language is misleading

A new contributor needs to know whether "functional" means:

* use `const`;
* use array methods;
* do not use classes;
* do not mutate caller-owned values;
* make all effects explicit;
* use typed error values;
* or some selected combination.

Today the answer is distributed across `AGENTS.md`,
the shared config,
five custom plugins,
a migration guide,
and several troubleshooting and planning documents.
A policy matrix would make the actual contract legible.

## Desired outcome

This is a policy and tracking issue.
It should not absorb the implementation already owned by #423,
#427,
or #453.
It should produce a coherent decision and open narrowly scoped child issues for any newly selected enforcement work.

The final policy should answer:

 1. Which owned boundaries promise deep readonly values?
 2. Which forms of local mutation are accepted,
    and what proves that mutable identity does not escape?
 3. Which effects require inference,
    a contract,
    a host-capability marker,
    or rejection?
 4. Are test helpers subject to the same semantic mutation policy as production helpers?
 5. What checked construct guarantees exhaustive handling of discriminated unions?
 6. Which function syntaxes are banned for a measured correctness reason rather than naming preference?
 7. When is a direct callback reference safe?
 8. When is Promise chaining semantically worse than `async`/`await`,
    and when is it merely another spelling?
 9. Are expected domain failures represented by thrown exceptions,
    typed values,
    or a boundary-specific mixture?
10. Which current rules should be renamed or documented as style rules rather than FP rules?

## Acceptance criteria

### Policy inventory

- [ ] Inventory every active and explicitly disabled FP-adjacent rule from the built configuration.
- [ ] Classify each rule as semantic guarantee,
      ownership boundary,
      correctness guard,
      architecture preference,
      syntax preference,
      formatting,
      or unrelated.
- [ ] Record what behavior each rule proves and what behavior remains possible after the rule passes.
- [ ] Record every production,
      test,
      declaration,
      generated-source,
      and self-hosting override affecting those rules.

### Target profile

- [ ] Publish a short repository decision defining binding immutability,
      value immutability,
      owned local mutation,
      effect transparency,
      composition,
      exhaustiveness,
      and error modeling.
- [ ] State deliberate departures from mainstream typed FP,
      including the exception-first and sentinel-first policies if retained.
- [ ] Give concrete accepted and rejected examples for parsers,
      collection builders,
      caches,
      callbacks,
      async resources,
      host objects,
      and domain failures.

### Semantic rollout boundaries

- [ ] Keep severity promotion of
      `no-readonly-parameter-mutations`,
      `no-opaque-parameter-effects`,
      and `no-invalid-parameter-effect-contracts`
      in #423.
- [ ] Resolve or explicitly accept the remaining #427 and #453 blockers before treating #423 as the semantic baseline.
- [ ] Decide whether `eslint/no-param-reassign` adds residual coverage after the semantic mutation rule is active.
- [ ] If value-level mutation needs new enforcement,
      file child issues scoped by ownership-known boundaries rather than a blanket mutation ban.

### Exhaustiveness

- [ ] Choose at least one checked exhaustive mechanism for discriminated unions.
- [ ] Prove the mechanism fails when a new union member is added without a handler.
- [ ] Re-evaluate the blanket `no-switch` rule only after the replacement mechanism exists.
- [ ] Ensure exact `Record` guidance uses the discriminant union as its key type
      and does not hide missing states behind a fallback.

### Syntax policy

- [ ] Re-evaluate `no-arrow-function`,
      `no-variable-function-expression`,
      callback-reference restrictions,
      and Promise-chain bans against named defect classes and positive controls.
- [ ] Retain each hard ban only when the accepted alternative removes a demonstrated defect
      or supplies a semantic guarantee.
- [ ] Separate naming and stack-trace preferences from mutation and purity claims in rule documentation.
- [ ] File independent child issues for any retained rule
      whose diagnostic suggests a rewrite that can weaken immutability or effect transparency.

### Verification and migration

- [ ] Establish a stable baseline for every semantic FP rule this issue retains or promotes.
- [ ] For each semantic guard,
      show a positive-control fixture that passes with the guard and fails when the guard is removed.
- [ ] Compare rule diagnostics with implementation branches so every promised effect path has coverage.
- [ ] Ratchet one semantic category at a time
      rather than adding further FP-related syntax bans to a 5,298-diagnostic workspace run.
- [ ] Record the final finding count and every reviewed exception before raising severity.
- [ ] Verify the selected rules through the built shared config and full workspace consumer boundary,
      not only through plugin unit tests.

## Non-goals

* Rewriting every imperative algorithm into chained array combinators.
* Banning all local mutation,
  `Map`,
  `Set`,
  parser cursors,
  or state machines.
* Replacing #423,
  #427,
  or #453.
* Selecting a third-party FP framework or effect system.
* Treating syntax counts as a purity metric.
* Weakening valid opacity findings for getters,
  `toJSON`,
  replacers,
  proxies,
  or unresolved host capabilities.
* Adding broad package overrides to make the workspace appear green.

## Related work and ownership boundaries

* #423 owns the workspace remediation,
  reviewed acceptance,
  self-hosting override,
  and direct-to-error promotion of the three extracted semantic rules.
* #427 owns remaining readonly analyzer correctness and diagnostic-classification defects.
* #453 records the current ergonomic-session remainder,
  including observer-return retention and the missing stable workspace fingerprint.
* #183 tracks functional composition helpers.
  Helpers can improve ergonomics,
  but they cannot substitute for mutation and effect guarantees.
* `doc/migration/no-class.md` owns the class-to-factory migration inventory and recipe.
* `package/config/oxlint/src/overrides.ts` is the current source of file-scope policy exceptions.

<!-- adjacent-unreviewed-20260914:logger-callbacks -->
## Review status

The local implementation and test changes described here **have not been reviewed**.
They are on `translation-repair-rebased`,
not an accepted change to main.

## Problem

While validating persisted preparation-input comparison,
a caller-provided logger throwing from `warn` prevented `failure.json` from being attempted and replaced the operation's names-only error.
A once-throwing test missed the persistent-warning case.

The comparison implementation still needs its integration fix.
This issue records the adjacent shared-logger work introduced for that fix,
without claiming the comparison is repaired.

## Local implementation

- `package/module/logger/src/observe-callbacks.ts` adds `observeLoggerCallbacks`.
- It forwards requested messages with lazy method lookup,
  the original receiver and unchanged ordering.
- It contains synchronous method/getter throws and explicit `flush` rejection,
  recording only fixed callback names in detached,
  frozen,
  canonical snapshots.
- It does not inspect or retain thrown values,
  retry messages,
  create a sink,
  or add a flush invocation.
- `src/index.ts` exports the utility and observation types.
- `src/observe-callbacks.unit.test.ts` exercises the built artifact,
  including getter/callable proxies,
  native Promise protocol faults,
  and snapshot immutability.

Relevant commits:
`fb0743f4439276d97b4a9485d20e2c8f618c2620`,
`ea3087d9c477b133df2b15bcaa401987d42bd78a`,
`9f052059351148bd1f851f09bcfe6a54afff38ab`,
`05bd5224baea0c8b3b292ac3bade3fa56866875f`,
`b38fa3917abea2735172950556187fb79c10d2cd`.

## Fixture defect encountered

Sinon 22.1.0 drops a thrown `undefined` in its proxy invocation path because rethrow is gated by `exception !== undefined`.
A stub factory returning undefined therefore did not inject the intended fault.

The local tests now use a suspended-start generator's native `throw` with a separate invocation counter.
A `caught` positive control proves the exact supplied value escapes before testing the observer.

Upstream already tracks this as sinonjs/sinon#2471 and PR sinonjs/sinon#2763.
No upstream duplicate or installed-dependency patch was made.

## Verification and limits

The native control on Node 26.8.2 observed a generator throwing undefined while the Sinon stub returned normally.
A selected-package run passed the logger unit suite after that fixture correction.
Subsequent native Promise-proxy fixtures and explicit catch-value discard passed type checking and the merged formatter;
a final full rerun remains pending.

These are tests,
not review.
The facade does not protect against callbacks that block,
exit the process,
mutate files,
or return an unobserved rejecting Promise from a void logging method.
A callback-name observation is not proof that a message was undelivered.

Related robustness work:
#479.
Comparison integration and final error/result observation ownership remain separate pending work.
rows.title: module-logger: unreviewed callback-observation workaround for throwing loggers

rows.body:
Remediating `@monochromatic-dev/module-translation-repair` took
`prefer-readonly-parameter-types` from 10 findings to 3. The seven that cleared
all had a workspace-owned producer, and the origin naming added in #424 pointed
at the correct edit every time; that part of the rule now works well and this
issue does not dispute it.

The three that remain, and one attribution defect I worked around, are below. All
were measured on commit `da3f2f4f9` of `translation-repair-rebased`.

Related but distinct: I left a summary on #423 covering the same ground before
knowing you wanted a standalone issue. This supersedes it and adds the extracted
rule measurements you asked about.

## 1. Foreign provenance does not survive a `.map` callback

Two of the three sit behind a `ForeignBorrowed` boundary that is already marked.
Marking it harder does not help, and I tested both placements.

`document-node.ts:180` has carried the marker on the PARAMETER since well before
this work:

```ts
export function buildDocumentNodes(
  {
    children,
  }: {
    readonly children: ForeignBorrowed<readonly RootContent[]>;
  },
): readonly DocumentNode[] {
  return children.map(function toDocumentNode(
    child,      // <- flagged
    index,
  ): DocumentNode {
```

reports:

        Parameter "child" can be deeply readonly: property type is writable. No
        workspace-owned source origin was proved for this inferred parameter
        type. Introduce an explicit deeply readonly type at the nearest
        project-owned boundary that supplies this callback value, then run type
        checking.

The nearest project-owned boundary is the parameter one line above, and it
already carries the marker.

I then tested the other placement, on a LOCAL rather than a parameter, at a
genuine host boundary in `stage-call.ts` where `Intl.Segmenter` returns its own
records:

```ts
const clusters: ForeignBorrowed<readonly Intl.SegmentData[]> = [
  ...new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: 'grapheme', },)
    .segment(flattened,),
];

const opening = clusters
  .slice(0, RAW_PREVIEW_CHARS,)
  .map(function toText(cluster,): string {   // <- still flagged
    return cluster.segment;
  },)
  .join('',);
```

The diagnostic is byte-identical before and after adding that annotation. Marker
on a parameter and marker on a local both fail the same way, which points at
provenance not reaching callback parameters of a method invoked on a
foreign-marked value, rather than at either placement being wrong.

`doc/troubleshooting/oxlint-prefer-readonly-foreign-provenance.md` lists
callbacks among the paths the propagation fix was built to carry, and names
`effect-binding-origins.ts` as carrying origins through properties, elements,
aliases, nested destructuring and `for...of` element bindings. Callback
parameters of a method call on a foreign-marked receiver may be the case that
list does not reach.

Note the rule does not say "this is foreign but I want more". It says no
workspace-owned origin was proved, which is the same message an unmarked value
gets, so from the diagnostic alone an author cannot tell that their marker was
seen and rejected versus never consulted.

## 2. An authored annotation cannot satisfy the rule when the type is not ours

`inspect-paragraph.ts:91` is different in kind: the type is authored, not
inferred.

```ts
function atomsOfNode({ node, }: { readonly node: RootContent; },): readonly ProtectedAtom[] {
```

        Destructured parameter with binding "node" can be deeply readonly:
        property type is writable. No exact syntax replacement was proved for
        this authored type. Make the reported writable path deeply readonly in
        its declaration or replace the annotation with a deeply readonly
        projection, then run type checking.

`readonly node` is already written. The writable path is `RootContent['type']`,
declared in `@types/mdast`, which this repo does not own and should not fork. So
of the two remedies offered, the first is not an action available here, and only
the projection is reachable.

I did not write the projection. Three bespoke recursive mapped types over
`@types/mdast` and `Intl.SegmentData`, across three unrelated files, existing
only to restate what upstream already means, satisfies the linter by making the
code worse. I also did not suppress, since
`no-restricted-syntax/no-disable-prefer-readonly-parameter-types` exists exactly
to stop that and is right to.

## 3. Origin attribution walks up to the enclosing callable for a reduce seed

Already worked around, but a different miss from the ones #424 fixed, so worth
recording separately.

`introduced-defect-probe.ts:190` flagged a `reduce` accumulator and named
`runIntroducedDefectProbe` at `introduced-defect-probe.ts:102` as its origin.
Line 102 is the exported function's signature line, not an expression that
produced a value. The real origin is the reduce SEED literal further down, whose
inferred type made every count writable.

The suggested edit, "give that callable an explicit deeply readonly return
type", would not have touched the cause: the callable named does not return the
accumulator. Naming the seed's type fixed it, so the REMEDY transferred, but the
LOCATION did not, and following the diagnostic literally would have been wasted
work.

## 4. Measurements of the three extracted rules

You mentioned these are recorded but off. I temporarily set all three to `error`
in `package/config/oxlint/src/rule/restriction.ts`, rebuilt the config, measured
this one package, and reverted. Numbers are from the type-aware wrapper run, not
a bare `oxlint` invocation; a bare one silently reports nothing for these rules
because they need `--type-aware`, which cost me one invalid null before I caught
it.

        base rule only                          3 errors
        all three extracted rules enabled     177 errors

Effectively all of the increase is `no-opaque-parameter-effects`.
`no-readonly-parameter-mutations` and `no-invalid-parameter-effect-contracts`
did not appear in the output at all for this package.

A representative message:

        The function input named "artifacts" is exposed to these unresolved
        calls: JSON.stringify [.../attribution-read.unit.test.ts:81].

        This rule cannot inspect enough of those calls to know what they might
        change. They could change the input itself, change an object stored
        inside it, call a function stored inside it, or arrange for one of those
        changes to happen later.

`JSON.stringify` driving a large share of these is worth a look before rollout.
It is in the default lib, it is famously non-mutating of its argument except
through a `toJSON` method or a replacer, and it appears constantly in test
fixtures. If it is treated as opaque, most of this package's test files
report.

## 5. The rule leaks internal errors with stack traces

The same run emitted 65 warnings of this shape, interleaved with findings:

        [warn] [effect-contract] semantic evidence unavailable for
        .../splice-slices.unit.test.ts: node-not-found: SemanticBridgeError:
        Owned effect edge lacks callee summary:
        .../splice-slices.unit.test.ts:967:2384:263.
            at assertReachedCallSummaries (.../plugin-prefer-readonly-parameter-type.mjs:4:65412)
            at ensureSource (...)
            ... eight more frames into the bundled plugin

Two problems independent of whether the underlying condition matters. A bundled
minified stack trace is not actionable by the person who ran the lint, and
"semantic evidence unavailable" means the rule silently analysed those files with
less information than it thought it had, which is a soundness question rather
than a formatting one: it is not clear whether findings are being missed on those
65 sites, or spuriously raised.

## What would resolve the three findings

Any of these, all outside the consuming package:

1.  Carry foreign provenance into callback parameters of methods invoked on a
    foreign-marked value. This alone clears two of the three.
2.  For an authored parameter whose writable path resolves into a declaration
    outside the workspace, either accept the annotation or report it distinctly,
    so the message does not prescribe an edit the author cannot make.
3.  Failing both, a config surface naming types whose declarations the workspace
    does not own. I looked for one in the rule source and its options and did not
    find one, which is why this is a report rather than a config change.

I left the `stage-call.ts` boundary marker in place even though it clears
nothing, because the ownership claim is true independently of whether the rule
reads it, and it makes the propagation gap reproducible from a checkout at
`c6bb1249d`.
rows.title: prefer-readonly-parameter-types: foreign provenance is lost through map callbacks, and three related defects

rows.body:
`rows.filter(observer).reduce(fold)` still reports, while `const kept = rows.filter(observer); kept.length` is clean. The difference is only that the container result is consumed directly as another call's receiver, which `resultEscapesCallable` counts as leaving the callable.

This is issue #414's own snippet in its chained form, so it is the shape a reader is most likely to try first.

## Measured

Built from `main` at the merge of `feat/readonly-collection-result-provenance`, summaries over an overlay source:

-    `plainFilterCount`, binding the result then reading `.length`: `mutated=[] opaque=[]`
-    `chainedFilterFold`, `slices.filter(stands).reduce(add, 0)`: `mutated=[] opaque=[0]`, cause `slices.filter`
-    `escapingFilter`, returning the filtered array: `mutated=[] opaque=[0]`, correctly

## Why it is precision rather than soundness

It reports where it could attribute. Nothing goes silent, and no offer is produced for a parameter anything writes, so the guarantee holds; the finding is just one a reader cannot act on without rewriting the chain into a binding.

## What would resolve it

`effect-result-escape.ts` enumerates the positions it treats as attributed. A member call whose receiver is the tracked result is analysed by the same pass that analyses any other collection call, so it is a candidate for that list rather than for the escape branch. The care needed is that the receiving call may itself be undischarged, in which case the report has to survive, which is what the receiver-side element origins added during the container discharge already arrange.

Related: #414.
rows.title: prefer-readonly-parameter-types: a collection call on a container receiver skips observer analysis

issue.body:
## Observed failure

The unchanged source TOML mutation task completes with exit zero,
green baseline and one source-terminal compileError mutant,
but the trial job fails an independent metadata observer.
No mutant assertion execution or full-campaign pass is claimed.

This repeated in run mj128hqwv0,
workflow t8wq69b56g,
job h4c49btlhq,
attempt 3wnf82gzb8,
source 525d2e09f8168a3bdd7e513e26d4c80b363123e5,
harness 0f8ad795aa92d3beb83e3bfa4e4aa54f1bea06f8.
The earlier bounded run 0j8zhbn9n0 retained the same null-status assertion without underlying operation details.

## Exact observer receipt

The command was container-bin/podman ps --all --filter label=io.monochromatic.toml-attempt=7185dde1-5802-43c2-b296-e257b9f313cf --format json,
working in the immutable source checkout.

It ran from 2026-10-17T07:25:23.786Z to 2026-10-17T07:25:31.793Z,
observed 8006.465648000001 milliseconds against an 8000-millisecond budget,
and returned null status,
SIGKILL,
ETIMEDOUT,
errno -110.
Stdout was three bytes ([] plus newline); stderr was zero bytes.
The wrapper assertion was null !== 0.

The generated Node container adapter forwards synchronously to sudo --non-interactive and the resolved actual Podman executable,
then propagates returned status after conditional cleanup.
An empty list on stdout does not establish wrapper or underlying Podman completion.
Podman,
sudo and Node lifecycle ownership remains unresolved; no database-lock or upstream lifecycle cause is claimed.
Seven other list operations and the final event query returned zero.
Source cleanup guards passed.

## Immutable evidence

Artifact 01a148c0-c29e-7644-a0ec-f546f5caf3e8 has 46389 bytes,
SHA-256 3e12339c854c28f69ef9ecdc29e03b2f1f0efe2959ad66bfd23347e1d75df2bb.
All 20 members are individually verified.
Exact operation JSONL,
source-native report,
shard identities,
before/after source proof,
logs and cleanup are retained in doc/audit/depot-toml-reconciliation-2026-10-17.evidence.json,
commit 7555eb5a89.
Provider interval 165116 milliseconds at 16x64 remains failed usage.

## Trial recovery and acceptance

The authorized metadata-only trial uses a 60000-millisecond bound,
an observer-only copied forwarder with before/after sudo lifecycle receipts,
and complete metadata durations.
The source consumer keeps the proven d098532a container adapter byte-for-byte and unchanged source arguments.
Disposable controls prove forwarding,
timeout rejection,
and detection after removing the timeout guard.
Actual bounded repeat vlrxjltfkq is dispatched at 316e1a8a309e71e456a741eb63e5ff3b94b75646.

Acceptance requires actual source completion,
all metadata operation receipts,
explicit forwarded results,
source correlation and scoped cleanup,
while preserving original failures and timeout rejection.
No application source change is included.
Full mutation completion remains separate.

## Duplicate search

All-state current-repository searches covered TOML metadata,
podman ETIMEDOUT,
and mutation observer.
Issue #1113 is the separate outer job timeout that lost active mutation evidence and censored an independent gate.
Issue #1114 concerns immutable input guards,
#1070 concerns the source logger sink timeout/SIGKILL,
and #1116/#1117 concern other container prerequisites.
No matching metadata-observer deadline incident was found.

The unchanged source command exits zero with a green baseline and the same source-terminal `compileError` identity.
No mutant assertion or full-campaign credit is claimed.
All ten metadata operations and every copied-forwarder sudo result return zero;
source correlation and scoped cleanup pass.
The slowest list call is `14100.441549` milliseconds,
of which `14077.079173` milliseconds is recorded inside synchronous sudo forwarding to `/usr/local/bin/podman`.
This establishes the forwarded span;
the underlying division between Podman and sudo remains unresolved.
The `60000`-millisecond bound covers this actual call.
Both original eight-second failures and timeout-rejection/removed-guard controls remain retained.

Artifact `01a148cd-37bb-750c-969a-1d040159af2e` is 55933 bytes,
SHA-256 `35ab60a4bbd6adb146676b810e3123d3d0fe08a2174873a73736480ee596be19`;
all 24 members are hash-verified.
Original consumer forwarder bytes are unchanged;
removing only the two observer lifecycle lines exactly reconstructs them.
Provider usage remains recorded as 165081 milliseconds at `16x64`.
Full immutable-source campaign completion is a separate boundary;
issue `#1113` remains open.
The complete observed recovery is retained in `doc/audit/depot-toml-reconciliation-2026-10-17.evidence.json`,
commit `a0b19dbfaf`.

control.disposableFault: Remove only the disposable Node forwarding executable after the actual compiler exits zero.

observedRepeat.state: Terminal fixture carrier failure before mutation assertions. The actual source gate invokes NanoSpawn, which inherits the parent eval flags and re-enters the control, producing EEXIST. No false-kill reproduction is claimed.

collection.scope: Read-only collection. Provider intervals require declared resources before pricing. Gate completion needs independent manifest reconciliation.

artifactIndex.extractionPolicy: Validated relative member names; unzip -p bytes are written as fresh regular files, never archive symlinks; 64MiB per-member and 128MiB total expansion bounds. Exact member counts and expanded byte sums are measured separately for each artifact.

## Status

The consumer-side changes have not been reviewed.
This tracks comparison cancellation ownership separately from logger callback observation in #509.
The repair is committed on `translation-repair-rebased`;
final qualification of its internal exports and combined terminal-warning control is in progress.
Do not close this issue based on tests or scoped review feedback alone.

## Reproduced failure

At `3707322f2`,
a genuine `AbortController.signal` with an own `aborted` getter could throw a comparison-shaped error.
`runProducerInputComparison` returned that caller's `storage` kind and foreign directory before preflight.
The owned error boundary was therefore incomplete despite initial request-value capture.

The retained `comparison-signal-origin-j3YwJS` probe on Node `26.8.2` observed the foreign directory
and `messageContainsCallerLocator: true`.
`devtest-bMMex9` records six ordinary failing assertions before the ownership repair.
`devtest-tlwWg1` separately records child creation before interruption setup could be trusted.
`devtest-Qm6PXT` records four later failing precedence/cleanup assertions.

## Implemented repair

- `producer-input-comparison-signal.ts` owns a live native signal,
  avoids caller state/reason/registration/removal overrides,
  preserves propagation resistance and ignores synthetic or replayed events.
- `producer-input-comparison-interrupt.ts` registers interruption before spawn,
  then attaches the child only after actual-close observation is active.
- `producer-input-comparison.ts` retains proven native cancellation over an unreadable observation,
  releases the subscription before terminal error decoration,
  and observes a fixed cleanup warning without replacing primary metadata.
- Existing production cancellation helpers are marked `@internal`
  and re-exported from the dedicated inert comparison barrel under `AGENTS.md` XPT.
  No general command executor or paid acquisition mode is added.

The source files are under `package/module/translation-repair/src/corpus-run/`.
Implementation commits include `2b5f8aebd`,
`bef628ba3`,
`1e45ca2cf`,
`9721f39d2` and `929f6671b`.
The last commit also adds combined cleanup-warning and built internal-export regressions.

## Evidence and remaining boundaries

The R6 artifact passed fresh builds,
types,
focused and full-unit checks,
read-only lint,
sealing,
mutation controls,
actual provider-free native cases and a relocated consumer.
The ledger distinguishes those bytes from the subsequent internal-export artifact.
Final qualification must also detect a terminal snapshot taken before a throwing cleanup warning.

Durable private evidence is under
`package/module/translation-repair/node_modules/.monochromatic/comparison-evidence/`.
The tracked ledger is `doc/planning/translation-repair-preparation-plan-and-journal-2026-09-14.md`.
The source trace and rejected approaches are in `doc/troubleshooting/node-abort-signal-owned-observation.md`.

This is a repository consumer-ownership defect,
not a claim that Node authenticates our operation metadata.
No Node issue or installed-dependency patch is proposed.
The checks do not establish hostile-runtime/internal-slot immunity,
whole-change review,
preparation approval or publication readiness.
No paid model invocation is part of this repair.
rows.title: module-translation-repair: unreviewed live cancellation ownership repair

Follow-up to #583, which fixed only the `errorOrThrow` docs.

## Settled: which detector

`Error.isError` is the repo's Error detector.
`no-restricted-syntax/prefer-error-is-error`
(`package/oxlint-plugin/no-restricted-syntax/src/rule/prefer-error-is-error.ts`)
flags four idioms and autofixes the plain cases:

```ts
// flagged idioms
value instanceof Error;
value.constructor === Error;
Object.prototype.toString.call(value) === '[object Error]';
util.types.isNativeError(value);
```

## Open: whether the current lint scope is right

The rule ships at `warn`, not `error`.
`package/config/oxlint/src/rule/restriction.ts:81` to `:84` says
"Initial severity is warn because the workspace has existing violations;
the rule autofixes ordinary cases for migration".
`ignorePatterns` (`package/config/oxlint/src/config-base.ts:63` onward) hides whole trees from it:
`**/package-paused/**`, `**/package-deprecated/**`, `**/*.js`, `**/*.cjs`,
`**/fixture/**`, `**/fixtures/**`, `**/invalid/**`, `**/test-fixture/**`,
`**/*.generated.ts`, `**/bundle`, `**/dist`.

Some exclusions look deliberate (rule fixtures),
some look incidental (embedded `mise.toml` task code is unlintable at any scope).
This issue is the evidence for the scope decision: every legacy Error detection site in the worktree,
grouped by why the lint does not see it today.
Nothing below is a prescribed fix; a site needs work only if its category comes into scope, or already is.

## How this list was gathered

```sh
# every occurrence in the worktree, including ignored trees
rg --no-ignore --hidden -n \
  "instanceof Error|isNativeError|\[object Error\]|constructor === Error|constructor !== Error" \
  --glob '!**/node_modules/**' --glob '!**/.git/**' --glob '!**/dist/**' --glob '!**/.cache/**' .
```

plus a duck-type sweep (`'message' in x`, `typeof x.message`),
then `git ls-files` / `git check-ignore --verbose` per hit to separate tracked sources
from ignored or generated artifacts.

## What the lint sees today (2 warnings)

`mise run lint:oxlint` at the repo root lints 4082 files and reports exactly 2 `prefer-error-is-error` warnings
(the run exits nonzero on unrelated pre-existing findings):

- `file-enforcer.config.ts:296`: `errorHasCode` guards with `error instanceof Error`.
- `package/module/conf-fork.fuzz/upstream-conf/index.ts:757`: vendored upstream migration code.
  This one may want a justified `oxlint-disable` rather than a rewrite, since it mirrors upstream.

## Sites no scope change reaches

- `package/config/tofu/mise.toml:110`: `malformedRecordRejected = error instanceof Error` inside a task body
  (`shell = "node --input-type=module-typescript -e"`).
  Oxlint only sees files, so `mise.toml` bodies escape every lint run regardless of `ignorePatterns`.
  Scope question: extract the body to a lintable module, or record these bodies as a known unlintable exception class.

## Categories hidden by `ignorePatterns`

Each category comes with the scope question it raises, not a fix plan.

### `**/package-paused/**` (22 sites in 20 files)

- `package-paused/desktop-daemon/editord/src/server/index-routes.ts:112`
- `package-paused/desktop-daemon/editord/src/server/lsp/lsp-manager-requests.ts:100`
- `package-paused/desktop-daemon/editord/src/server/operations/write-file-atomic.ts:135`
- `package-paused/desktop-daemon/editord/src/server/ws-send.ts:27`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/container-base.ts:164`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/linter-exec.ts:43`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/mise.migrate-labels.ts:154`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/runner-failure.ts:81`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/runner-probe-artifacts.ts:274`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/runner-probe-fix.ts:182`
- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary-viewer/src/data/read-artifacts.ts:61`
- `package-paused/webapp-content/messages-demo/src/client/composer/send.ts:120`
- `package-paused/webapp-content/messages-demo/src/client/composer.worker.ts:132`
- `package-paused/webapp-content/messages-demo/src/client/composer.worker.ts:460`
- `package-paused/webapp-content/messages-demo/src/client/editor/buffer.worker.ts:264`
- `package-paused/webapp-content/messages-demo/src/server/api/import.ts:230`
- `package-paused/webapp-edu/paper2vn/src/client/screens/lecture-ask.ts:243`
- `package-paused/webapp-edu/paper2vn/src/client/screens/select-topic.ts:153`
- `package-paused/webapp-edu/paper2vn/src/smoke.ts:253`
- `package-paused/webapp-forge/server/src/git/iso-server.ts:224`
- `package-paused/webapp-forge/server/src/git/iso-server-refs.ts:287`
- `package-paused/webapp-forge/server/src/git/iso-server-refs.ts:304`

Scope question: the tree is paused, and `config-base.ts:75` to `:79` also cites a two-rule autofix oscillation
in one file there (see `doc/troubleshooting/oxlint-multi-fix-convergence.md`).
Does the pause justify staying excluded, or should resumed work land clean?

### `**/package-deprecated/**` (3 sites)

- `package-deprecated/mcp/nvim/src/oxlint-spawn.ts:133`
- `package-deprecated/mcp/nvim/src/tool-get-all-diagnostics.ts:134`
- `package-deprecated/mcp/nvim/src/tool-get-diagnostics.ts:188`

Scope question: deprecated tree; staying excluded looks consistent, but that is a scope call, not a fact.

### `**/*.js` (and `.gitignore:57` `*.js`)

5 sites each in `package/music-player/design/support.js` (`:929`, `:952`, `:1088`, `:1244`, `:1721`)
and `package/music-player/design/candidates/support.js` (same lines).
Both files are untracked local scratch (`git check-ignore` matches `.gitignore:57:*.js`).
Scope question: they only matter if they become tracked; browser runtime support for `Error.isError`
would need checking before any change there.

### Duck-typed caught-error check (no rule covers this shape at any scope)

- `package/pi-plugin/advisor/src/advisor-completion.ts:307` to `:312`:
  extracts `error.message` through `typeof error === 'object' && 'message' in error`,
  so it also accepts plain `{ message }` objects.

Scope question: should the rule grow a duck-type detector, or does this site change on its own merits?
Separate from the ignore-pattern decisions.

## Generated, fixture, and local artifacts (evidence only, not fix targets)

- `package-paused/dev-script/inference-canary/src/canary-lint/` (gitignored via `.gitignore:90` `canary-lint/`):
  108 recorded model-run files (`canary.ts`, `response.txt`, `meta.json`) containing the idiom.
  Recorded outputs, not maintained code.
- `package/desktop-daemon/hall-monitor/index.js.map` (gitignored via `.gitignore:58` `*.map`):
  stale generated source map whose embedded `sourcesContent` shows `src/infra/notification.ts`
  and `src/cycle.ts` with the idiom, while both files on disk now call `caughtValueText`.
  Regenerate rather than edit.
- `doc/planning/promises-teaching*.local.html` (gitignored via `.gitignore:11` `*.local.*`):
  6 local planning artifacts with 9 to 11 occurrences each.

## Doc snippets with the idiom (prose, optional)

- `doc/dependency-blocklist.md:401` (probe command)
- `doc/troubleshooting/npm-cli-parsers-partial-git-argv.md:219`
- `doc/troubleshooting/pi-advisor-long-session-provider-failure.md:250`
- `doc/troubleshooting/pi-synthetic-provider-startup-model-scope.md:119`
- `doc/troubleshooting/rolldown-1-2-typescript-trust-tsconfig-discovery.md:505`
- `doc/troubleshooting/sinon-context-owned-stubs.patch:166` and `:247`
  (patch against sinon upstream tests)

Some reproduce upstream or external code and should stay literal.

## Deliberate exceptions at any scope (must not change)

- `package/oxlint-plugin/no-restricted-syntax/src/rule/prefer-error-is-error.ts`
  and siblings (`prefer-error-is-error.detectors.ts`, `.node-util.ts`, `.object-tag.ts`, `.syntax.ts`, `.globals.ts`),
  plus `package/oxlint-plugin/no-restricted-syntax/src/oxlint-no-restricted-syntax.unit.test.ts`:
  the rule and its tests.
- `package/test-fixture/oxlint-no-restricted-syntax/src/valid/prefer-error-is-error.ts`
  and `package/test-fixture/oxlint-no-restricted-syntax/src/invalid/prefer-error-is-error.ts`:
  rule fixtures (`**/test-fixture/**` and `**/invalid/**` are lint-ignored on purpose).

## Subclass checks: never targets for this rule

These discriminate subclasses (`instanceof TypeError`, `instanceof RangeError`, `instanceof ParseError`),
which `Error.isError` cannot do; the rule cannot replace them and no scope change makes it able to:

- `package/git-policy/markdown-lint/src/rewrite-candidates.ts:449`
- `package/module/conf-fork.fuzz/src/store-adapters.ts:309`
- `package/module/conf-fork/src/errors.unit.test.ts:141`, `:154`, `:198`, `:211`, `:224`, `:237`
- `package/module/deepmerge-ts.fuzz/src/mutation-canon.ts:171`
- `package/module/deepmerge-ts.fuzz/src/recall-ledger-runtime.ts:253`
- `package/module/matcher-fork.fuzz/src/limits.property.unit.test.ts:205`
- `package/module/p-limit-fork.fuzz/src/limits.property.unit.test.ts:236`
- `package/module/pify-fork.fuzz/src/pify-adapters.ts:107`
- `package/module/toml-edit.fuzz/src/parse-toml-edit.property.unit.test.ts:206`
- Fork packages documenting caller reliance on `instanceof TypeError`,
  each at `src/errors.ts:5`:
  `package/module/quick-lru-fork`, `package/module/matcher-fork`,
  `package/module/p-memoize-fork`, `package/module/p-limit-fork`, `package/module/pify-fork`

## Decision checklist

1. Per category above: in scope or out, and why (fixtures and deprecated trees may correctly stay out).
2. Whatever lands in scope gets fixed or carries a justified `oxlint-disable` comment.
3. Only then consider raising `no-restricted-syntax/prefer-error-is-error` from `warn` to `error`
   at `package/config/oxlint/src/rule/restriction.ts:84`.
rows.title: prefer-error-is-error: is the lint scope right? full legacy Error detection inventory

## What to build

Let several `git commit` invocations against the same worktree and branch run at the same time, and land each as its own sequential commit, instead of failing every overlapping commit after the first with `index.lock` `EEXIST` (the #560 collision).

Accepted design: `doc/decision/cli-git-concurrent-commits.md` on branch `feat/cli-git-concurrent-commits`. Evidence and per-question rationale: `doc/planning/cli-git-concurrent-commits.md`. Execution record: `doc/handover/cli-git-concurrent-commits.md`.

Work happens in the `feat/cli-git-concurrent-commits` worktree and merges to `main` after verification.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Per-transaction journals; startup recovery handles every prepared, reserved, or landing transaction, including crashed owners.
- [ ] Parallel preparation: native `git commit` against a private index and private admin dir `HEAD`, pending commit protected by a `refs/cli-git/` ref, hooks through the dispatcher shim (absolute `GIT_WORK_TREE`, `post-commit` held back, config-based hooks covered, no shell scripts).
- [ ] Per-repository hook lock by default; `hooks: { concurrentCommits: true }` opts into parallel hooks.
- [ ] Serial landing: landing lock plus real `index.lock`, compare-and-swap ref update with nonce reflog message, real index computed at landing, unmoved `HEAD` lands the prepared commit itself.
- [ ] Replay via `git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base` and `git commit-tree` (re-signed when signed); conflicts fail as `core-finding` exit `1` naming paths and the winning commit.
- [ ] `--amend`, merge/cherry-pick/revert conclusions, and branch switches fail when `HEAD` or its symbolic target moved.
- [ ] Policy `inputs?: 'unrestricted' | { external: PolicyInput[] }` (default `'unrestricted'`), lazy read-set tracking, fingerprinted external inputs; shipped plugins declare their inputs.
- [ ] `pre-commit` re-runs outside the landing lock when the replayed tree differs; `post-commit` runs once after landing with native-equivalent env.
- [ ] Reservation after `landing.reserveAfterLostRaces` lost races (default 2).
- [ ] `core.lockfilePid=true` injected into every forwarded and spawned Git; proven-live `index.lock` owners get unbounded waits; others get Git-style backoff up to `indexLock.unprovenOwnerTimeoutMs` (default 1000); cli-git never deletes a lock.
- [ ] Forwarded index writers wait under the same rules and re-forward only when fixtures prove failure before side effects; `git cli-git fix` holds the landing lock across install and verification.
- [ ] Single-flight auto-push per branch; each commit exits only once the remote contains its OID.
- [ ] No opt-out switch.
- [ ] Disposable real-Git fixtures and packed shadow-bin fixtures for concurrent commits, replay, conflicts, crashes, hooks, and locks; concurrent-commit lifecycle benchmark confirms the reservation default.
- [ ] Container end-to-end suite, inherent to verifying concurrent mutation of shared Git state (unit and shadow-bin fixtures cannot show interleavings, crash recovery, or lock contention): a mise task packs the tarball and runs inside bounded `podman` against freshly created dummy repositories and a local bare remote, at the minimum and current Git versions, replaying realistic workloads (commit-shape traces mined from this repository's history plus a concurrent-agent scenario catalog: shared-file hunks, interleaved index writers, hookdir/config/stash hooks, signing, amend, branch switch, foreign lock holders, `gc --prune=now`, `SIGKILL` at every phase). Seeded and replayable; invariants checked after every run (each successful commit lands once with its captured bytes, no lost edits, no staged reverts, remote has every landed OID, no leftover refs/transactions/locks, `git fsck` clean, exit codes match JSONL).
- [ ] `SPEC.md` and `README.md` describe the new protocol, config keys, `inputs`, and JSONL events.
rows.title: feat(cli-git): land concurrent commits with parallel preparation and serial landing

Follow-up from `doc/decision/private-npm-registry.md` ("Verification").

The first rollout of the private pnpr registry (`https://pnpr.c.aquati.cat/~monochromatic-dev/`) only verifies, from a throwaway consumer:

- anonymous install and use of `@monochromatic-dev/oxlint-plugin-tsdoc`, `@monochromatic-dev/config-typescript`, and `@monochromatic-dev/module-or-throw`;
- install of `@monochromatic-dev/module-logger`;
- that a publish without the OIDC workload credential is rejected, and the workflow's OIDC publish succeeds.

The other published packages (128 qualified on 2026-09-14: every workspace package outside `package/test-fixture/` whose manifest declares `exports`, `main`, `module`, or `bin`) are not checked.

## Task

Blocked until the registry is deployed (`doc/runbook/deploy-pnpr-registry.md`) and the first publish run completes.

- In a throwaway consumer that routes `@monochromatic-dev` to pnpr and adds `@monochromatic-dev/*` to `minimumReleaseAgeExclude`, install every package pnpr serves, one at a time.
- For each package with a runtime entry point, import or execute it under Node; for type-only or TypeScript-source packages, type-check an import.

- Decide per failure whether to fix the manifest or add the package to the reviewed exclusion list.

## Status

Plan drafted and posted: https://github.com/Aquaticat/Monochromatic/issues/247#issuecomment-4887670850 (scope grew beyond the body below: ground-up rewrite as packages/cli/mutation-test with sharded disposable containers; the plan comment supersedes the rough shape here). Implementation in progress.

## Motivation

Own the mutation tester the same way `@monochromatic-dev/module-test` replaced Vitest, and shed the StrykerJS + Babel dependency footprint entirely.

This is not about `convert-source-map`. That transitive edge is already neutralized and inert: Stryker's instrumenter is parse-only and never enters Babel's `transform` pipeline (the only place `@babel/core` requires `convert-source-map`), so the throwing stub is never loaded at runtime. See `docs/troubleshooting/dependencies.md` (the `convert-source-map` deep-dive) and `docs/troubleshooting/stryker-container-runtime.md`. The driver here is footprint and control, not a runtime bug.

## Goal

A container-native mutation testing framework, built on oxc, that replaces the Stryker-spawn core of `@monochromatic-dev/dev-script-mutation-test`, reusing that package's existing orchestration.

Container-native means the engine is designed to run inside the existing per-source Podman container (worktree, isolation, resource caps, no network), not as a host tool wrapped to look containerized. It integrates with the current container worktree, source/test selection, and JSON reporting rather than assuming a host runtime.

No Babel. The whole `@babel` subtree goes away; oxc owns parsing.

## Rough shape (to be designed, not prescriptive)

- Parse with oxc (`oxc-parser`). Locate mutable nodes by their source spans and apply each mutation by splicing replacement text at the node's byte offsets, which avoids a separate code-generation step entirely. Fall back to oxc transform/codegen only if span-splicing proves insufficient for some operator.
- Mutation operators reimplemented against oxc's ESTree-style AST, covering the same families as the ~15 Stryker mutators (arithmetic, equality, logical, conditional, boolean, string, unary, update, array, object, optional chaining, block statement, method expression, arrow function, regex).
- Per-mutant generate-and-run against `module-test` with kill detection (killed / survived / timeout / error), instead of mutation-switching.
- Optional TypeScript type-check filter to drop non-compiling mutants (Stryker's typescript-checker value-add). This is the hardest, riskiest piece and needs incremental tsc for acceptable speed.
- Reuse the existing container isolation, source/test selection, and report aggregation in `packages/dev-script/mutation-test/src` as-is.

## Measured baselines

- `packages/dev-script/mutation-test/src`: 3,516 code lines; only 218 are Stryker-spawn glue (`stryker-config.ts`, `container-stryker.ts`, `inline-nu.ts`). The other ~3,300 (container, selection, reporting, CLI, runtime image) is reusable.
- `packages/module/test/src` precedent: 2,829 code lines.
- `@stryker-mutator/instrumenter` (engine to reimplement, complexity proxy only; we port operator logic, not Babel-specific code): 2,447 compiled lines (mutators 566, mutant-placers 215, transformers 374, parsers 422, util 341, top-level 307, printers 71, frameworks 88).
- Footprint dropped: 5 `@stryker-mutator` packages and the entire `@babel` subtree (~44 packages). oxc replaces parsing; span-splicing removes the need for a JS code generator.

## LoC estimate (engineering estimate, not measured)

- Minimum viable, no type-check filter: ~1,100 production + ~700 test new code lines; net production delta ~+900 after deleting the 218 glue lines. (oxc span-splicing keeps the parse/codegen glue small, since no generator is written.)
- Feature parity, with type-check filter: ~1,500 production + ~900 test new code lines.
- In raw file lines (TSDoc-everywhere house style, ~0.6 to 0.7 comments per code line): roughly 2,900 to 3,800 raw lines across new files.

## References

- `docs/troubleshooting/dependencies.md`
- `docs/troubleshooting/stryker-container-runtime.md`
- `packages/dev-script/mutation-test/`
- `packages/module/test/` (precedent)
rows.title: Replace Stryker with our own container-native mutation testing framework (no plan drafted yet)

## Status: approved (2026-06-10)

Resolved via a grilling session; see the resolution comment below for the decided design. The original A/B/C framing in the plan doc is superseded. Implementation has not started.

## Plan document

See `docs/migration/mise-nushell-to-node.md` (committed locally as `f82d872d`, pending push to the remote).

## Summary

We are migrating the repo's primary runtime to Node. This issue tracks the question of whether to set mise's task shell to Node and migrate every task body off nushell.

Key constraint, verified on Node `v26.3.0`: an inline shell of `node -e` evaluates the body as JavaScript. It handles TS type stripping, ESM imports, top-level await, and fail-fast cleanly, but a plain command line such as `cargo build --release` is not valid JS and would have to be routed through `node:child_process`. Most of the repo's task bodies are exactly such command runners.

Measured scope: 121 `mise.toml` files, 74 with inline `run`, 263 inline bodies. Only ~8 files carry real nushell logic (root, terminal, tofu, music-player, forbidden-strings, rust); the rest are command runners.

## Decisions needed before any work starts

- Which approach: B (logic to Node-run `mise.*.ts`, command runners stay shell; recommended), A (literal `node -e` everywhere), or C (Node shell-in-JS layer such as zx). Plan ranks B > C > A.
- File-task interpreter policy: `#!/usr/bin/env node` shebang, `use_file_shell_for_executable_tasks = true`, or non-executable `.ts`.
- Whether file-enforcer's own `bun` invocation moves to `node` in the same migration.

## Follow-ups bundled in the plan

- Flip the four `*_default_*_shell_args` settings only after bodies are converted.
- Remove the `aqua:nushell/nushell` pin and update stale "primary runtime"/"Bun shell" comments.
- Rewrite AGENTS.md `CM2` and `SCR`, which currently mandate nushell.
rows.title: Plan: migrate mise task shell from nushell to Node (approved)
